Languages of antiquity

Japan: Chinese characters and kana

The Japanese islands · from the first inscriptions in the 5th century to the women writers of the Heian period

At a glance

Region
the Japanese islands; the centre of the state lay around Nara and Kyoto
Period
first inscriptions 5th century; Nara 710–794, Heian 794–1185
Language
Old Japanese, later Classical Japanese (Japonic family); over 120 million speakers today
Script
Chinese characters (kanji), and from them man'yōgana, hiragana and katakana; the Latin alphabet from the 16th century
Earliest books
Kojiki (712), Nihon Shoki (720), Man'yōshū (after 759)
Today
kanji, hiragana and katakana in the same text; 2,136 common characters (list of 2010)

The Japanese took their writing from China, although their language has nothing in common with Chinese. At first they wrote in Chinese, then learned to read Chinese texts as Japanese, and finally began to use Chinese characters for their sound alone. From this script, called man'yōgana, two syllabaries arose in the 9th century: flowing hiragana from cursive writing and angular katakana from fragments of characters. Court ladies of the Heian period wrote works such as the Tale of Genji in hiragana. Modern Japanese combines Chinese characters with both kana, which makes it one of the most complex writing systems in the world.

A script from the mainland

Japan encountered Chinese writing before it began to use it. According to Chinese annals, in AD 57 Emperor Guangwu of Han granted a gold seal to an envoy from the Japanese land of Na. Objects bearing Chinese characters appear on the islands from the 1st century, but by the prevailing view regular writing began only in the 5th century. Both the Kojiki and the Nihon Shoki state that writing and Chinese books were brought by scholars from the Korean kingdom of Baekje; there is no direct evidence, but scholars generally accept it.

The oldest inscriptions made in Japan are Chinese texts, probably written by immigrant scribes. The best known is the sword from the Inariyama burial mound, excavated in 1968: X-rays in 1978 revealed a gold-inlaid inscription of at least 115 characters. It is dated to a shinkai year, by the prevailing interpretation 471, and the Japanese personal names in it are written phonetically, with characters used only for their sound. Similar inscriptions appear on the Eta Funayama sword and the Suda Hachiman Shrine mirror.

The decisive impulse came with Buddhism, which reached Japan from Korea in the 6th century. It brought sacred texts (sutras) written in Chinese, temples became centres of learning, and Chinese became the language of government, religion and scholarship, much as Latin was in medieval Europe. Texts written in Chinese are called kanbun in Japan; until modern times perhaps more of them were produced there than texts in Japanese.

Reading Chinese as Japanese

Japanese differs from Chinese in structure. A Chinese word is usually a single uninflected syllable and the sentence runs subject – verb – object. Japanese words often have several syllables, verbs are conjugated with suffixes, grammatical relations are marked by particles placed after words, and the verb stands at the end of the sentence. The Japanese therefore learned to read Chinese text directly as Japanese, a method called kanbun kundoku: the reader rearranged the words into Japanese order, added Japanese endings and particles, and read the characters as Japanese words of the same meaning.

Small marks added to the text (kunten) served this purpose: dots at the edges of characters, return marks (kaeriten) showing the order in which the characters are to be read, and later small syllabic signs for the endings. The earliest securely dated Japanese examples of return marks are from 783 and 788. The method has survived to this day: Japanese secondary schools teach kanbun as part of language education, and a single standard for the marks has applied since 1912.

For the same reason most characters have two kinds of reading in Japanese. The on reading (on'yomi) imitates the Chinese pronunciation of the character at the time the character and its word were borrowed, and is used mainly in words of Chinese origin. The kun reading (kun'yomi) is the native Japanese word matching the character's meaning. The character 人 “person” is read hito in Japanese but jin in Chinese compounds; the character 行 is read i in iku “to go”, okona in okonau “to carry out”, gyō in gyōretsu “line”, kō in ginkō “bank” and an in andon “lantern”. Because Chinese words were borrowed at different times and from different regions, a character may have several on readings.

Characters for sounds: man'yōgana

Names, poems and Japanese endings could not be written in Chinese. Scribes therefore began to use Chinese characters for their sound alone, regardless of meaning, as the Chinese and Koreans had earlier done with foreign place and personal names. In Japan this grew into a complete syllabic script called man'yōgana. Characters were read either by their Chinese pronunciation (for example 波 for ha) or by a Japanese word (the character 女 “woman” for the syllable me). There were no fixed rules: by the end of the 8th century some 970 different characters were used for about 90 syllables of Japanese, and for the syllable ka alone the Man'yōshū uses almost twenty.

The oldest Japanese books were produced at the imperial court in Nara in the early 8th century. The Kojiki (“Records of Ancient Matters”), completed in 712, tells of the creation of the world, the gods and the first emperors; its prose is written in Chinese characters with a Japanese-influenced structure, while its 112 songs are written phonetically. The Nihon Shoki (“Chronicles of Japan”) of 720 is written in Chinese on the model of Chinese histories, but its 128 songs are also in man'yōgana.

The script takes its name from the Man'yōshū (“Collection of Ten Thousand Leaves”), the oldest surviving anthology of Japanese poetry. It has 20 books and over 4,500 poems, among them 4,207 short poems (tanka) and 265 long ones (chōka); the last datable poem is from 759. Its last compiler was, by the prevailing view, the poet Ōtomo no Yakamochi. The poems were written by emperors and courtiers but also by frontier guards and people from the eastern provinces, so the collection records eastern dialects too. The Man'yōshū mixes characters used for sound with characters used for meaning, and it is still difficult to read.

Writing outside the court is documented by mokkan, wooden tags and slips. Officials wrote notes, letters and lists on them and attached them to shipments of taxes. More than 150,000 from the late 7th and early 8th centuries have been excavated. Their language is more colloquial than that of the poems, and they show that a fairly large number of officials could already write. Three of the tags carry poems that also appear in the Man'yōshū.

Old Japanese

The language of the Nara period (710–794) is called Old Japanese. Like modern Japanese it was agglutinative: suffixes and particles were added to the stem, the verb came at the end of the sentence and modifiers preceded the noun. Syllables were simple, usually a consonant and a vowel, and a word could not begin with r or a voiced consonant. Modern h was originally pronounced p (the syllable ha, written with 波, sounded pa); whether it was still a p in the Nara period or already a bilabial f is disputed.

Careful analysis of man'yōgana shows that the scribes of the oldest texts distinguished 88 syllables, more than later Japanese. For the syllables ki, hi, mi, ke, he, me, ko, so, to, no, yo, ro (and in the Kojiki also mo) they always used one set of characters for certain words and another set for other words. The phenomenon is called jōdai tokushu kanazukai, and the two series are labelled kō (A) and otsu (B) after Japanese cyclical signs. The linguist Shinkichi Hashimoto described it systematically in the early 20th century; the distinction disappeared during the Heian period.

What exactly the difference meant is debated and there is no consensus. The traditional interpretation, put forward by Kyōsuke Kindaichi in 1938, is that Old Japanese had eight vowels instead of today's five: besides i, e and o there were three more, pronounced further towards the centre of the mouth. Others, especially since the work of Roland Lange in 1968, explain the difference as diphthongs or as the glides y and w before or after the vowel. Internal reconstruction points, on the contrary, to an earlier stage with fewer vowels.

Most texts record the language of the court at Nara, Western Old Japanese. Poems from the eastern provinces in Books 14 and 20 of the Man'yōshū show an eastern dialect with different forms and with loanwords from Ainu. Some of its features survive in the Hachijō language, spoken on the Hachijō islands south of Tokyo.

The oldest books in manuscript

Kana: a script from cursive and from fragments

Writing Japanese with dozens of complex characters was slow, and during the 9th century the characters used for sound were simplified. Two syllabaries arose, together called kana. Hiragana (“plain kana”) grew out of man'yōgana written in a very fluid cursive (sōsho): each hiragana sign is a simplified whole Chinese character, for example あ from 安. Katakana (“partial kana”) arose by keeping only part of a character written in regular script, usually its first or last few strokes: カ is the left half of 加.

Katakana was created by Buddhist monks in Nara. They wrote it small between the lines of sutras written in Chinese to indicate the Japanese reading and endings, so katakana began as a reading aid. Koreans used similar abbreviated parts of characters (the gugyeol script), and some katakana signs resemble them in shape. The two kana sometimes derive from the same character (か and カ from 加), sometimes from different ones (る from 留, ル from 流).

Tradition credits the invention of kana to the Buddhist monk Kūkai (774–835), founder of the Shingon school, who returned from China in 806 with knowledge of the Indian Siddhaṃ script. This cannot be proved; kana developed gradually and at many hands. Indian phonetics did, by the prevailing view, shape the order of syllables in the gojūon (“fifty sounds”) table: the vowels a, i, u, e, o and the consonants k, s, t, n, h, m, y, r, w follow one another much as in the Sanskrit alphabet. The order is first attested in a Japanese text in the 12th century.

For a long time each syllable could be written with several signs. Hiragana received a single standard form only in the school reform of 1900, which chose one variant for each syllable; the others are now called hentaigana (“variant kana”) and appear only in decorative writing.

夜久毛多都ya-kumo tatu (Old Japanese)“many clouds rise”, the first line of the first song in the Kojiki (712). Each character stands only for its Chinese pronunciation and its meaning plays no part: 夜 “night”, 久 “long”, 毛 “fur”, 多 “many”, 都 “capital”. This is the man'yōgana from which both kana developed.

Hiragana, katakana and Chinese characters are set in Noto Serif JP, with the characters in their Japanese forms. Each box shows the source Chinese character on the left and the kana on the right. The origins follow the usual account; other models have been proposed for some, for example both 川 and 州 for つ and ツ. Values are given in Hepburn romanization.

The writing of court ladies

In the Heian period (794–1185), named after the new capital Heian-kyō, today's Kyoto, men's official writing remained Chinese and the regular script of characters, called otokode (“men's hand”). Hiragana instead took hold in private letters and poetry, and because it was used above all by women, who were usually denied a Chinese education, it was called onnade, “women's hand”. It allowed court ladies to write as people spoke, and they created the first great works of Japanese prose.

Yet hiragana was not only for women. In 905 Emperor Daigo ordered the compilation of the Kokin Wakashū (“Collection of Ancient and Modern Poems”), the first anthology of Japanese poems (waka) compiled by imperial command. One of its compilers, the poet Ki no Tsurayuki, wrote a Japanese preface in kana (kanajo) alongside the Chinese one. Around 935 the same Tsurayuki wrote the Tosa Diary, describing the journey back to the capital from Tosa Province, where he had been governor. He wrote it in hiragana, as if it were written by a woman in his party.

The summit of Heian prose is the Tale of Genji (Genji monogatari) by a lady-in-waiting known to us only by the nickname Murasaki Shikibu. The 54-chapter novel, written in the early 11th century mostly in hiragana, tells of the life and loves of the emperor's son Genji and his descendants, and is often called one of the first novels in world literature. From about the same time comes the Pillow Book (Makura no sōshi) of the court lady Sei Shōnagon. Both authors knew Chinese writing, but they did not have to write in it.

The man who wrote as a woman

The Tosa Diary (Tosa nikki) opens with the sentence: “Diaries are written by men, I hear; now a woman will try her hand at one.” Diaries were kept by officials at the time, and in Chinese. By the prevailing interpretation Ki no Tsurayuki hid behind a female narrator so that he could write in Japanese and in hiragana, more personally and with the poems he included in the diary, among them grief for a daughter who had died in Tosa. The diary is among the oldest works of Japanese prose written in kana and is usually seen as an influence on the later diaries of court ladies.

The iroha poem

For a long time the order of syllables was learned not from a table but from the iroha poem, named after its first three syllables. The poem is a pangram: each of the 47 syllables of the time occurs in it exactly once, including wi (ゐ) and we (ゑ), which disappeared from standard spelling only in 1946. The syllable n (ん) is missing, because it did not yet have a sign of its own and was written like mu.

Tradition attributes the poem to Kūkai, but the attribution is no longer accepted. The poem no longer distinguishes the vowel e from the syllable ye, which earlier Japanese still had, and it is therefore most often dated to the 10th or 11th century. The oldest surviving copy is from 1079. Its content is Buddhist: by the usual interpretation it paraphrases a verse on the impermanence of all things from the Nirvana Sutra.

Dictionaries ordered syllables by the iroha until modern times, and it is still sometimes used to number items in a list. In music the syllables i, ro, ha, ni, ho, he, to (in katakana イロハニホヘト) name the notes A to G, so ハ長調, ha chōchō, is C major. The usual order of syllables today, however, is gojūon.

Three scripts in one sentence

Modern Japanese text mixes three scripts. Kanji write the roots of words, hiragana endings, particles and words without a common character, and katakana loanwords, foreign names, onomatopoeia and the names of animals and plants. In the sentence 私はビールを飲みます (watashi wa bīru o nomimasu, “I drink beer”) the characters 私 “I” and 飲 “drink” are kanji, the particles は and を and the ending みます are in hiragana, and ビール “beer”, borrowed from Dutch, is in katakana. Czech names are written in katakana too: プラハ Puraha is Prague, ヴァーツラフ広場 Vātsurafu hiroba Wenceslas Square.

After 1945 the script underwent a major reform. In 1946 kana spelling was brought into line with actual pronunciation (gendai kanazukai) and the government limited the characters for general use to 1,850 (tōyō kanji); many characters were given simplified shapes (shinjitai). Since 1981 a recommended list, the jōyō kanji, has replaced the binding limit; it was extended to 2,136 characters in 2010, and pupils learn 1,026 of them by the end of the sixth grade. The total number of characters ever used in Japanese exceeds 50,000.

The Japanese first met the Latin alphabet (rōmaji) in the 16th century through Portuguese traders and missionaries; the first romanization of Japanese, based on Portuguese spelling, was devised around 1548 by a Japanese Christian named Anjirō. Today the most common system is Hepburn romanization, named after the American missionary James Curtis Hepburn and adapted to English (shi, chi, tsu, ji); alongside it there is the official Kunrei system (si, ti, tu, zi). Czech has its own transcription based on Czech pronunciation (ši, či, cu, dži, ja, jo), which is why Czech writes Murasaki Šikibu and Kodžiki where English has Murasaki Shikibu and Kojiki.

Japanese words around the world

Many Japanese words have passed into English and other languages. Words written in kanji can be taken apart into elements with meanings of their own:

JapaneseanalysisEnglish
着物 kimonoki(ru) “to wear” + mono “thing”: “something worn”kimono
津波 tsunamitsu “harbour” + nami “wave”tsunami

The Japonic languages

Japanese belongs to the Japonic family. Besides Japanese and its dialects, the family includes the Hachijō language and the Ryukyuan languages of the Ryukyu Islands between Kyushu and Taiwan, such as Okinawan, Miyako, Yaeyama and Yonaguni. The Ryukyuan languages preserve some features older than those of the Old Japanese of Nara. They are not mutually intelligible with Japanese, but in Japan they have traditionally been regarded as its dialects. Most of them are now severely endangered.

No relationship between the Japonic languages and any other family has been proved. The most studied hypotheses link them to Korean or to the so-called Altaic languages, or posit Austronesian influence. Modern Japanese and Korean have very similar sentence structure, but the earlier stages of the two languages differ so much that most scholars do not consider a common origin established.

Also unrelated is Ainu, the language of the indigenous people of Hokkaido, Sakhalin and the Kurils, regarded as an isolate; it has its own card in the atlas. Eastern Old Japanese borrowed a number of words from it. Ainu is now often written in katakana extended with small signs for syllable-final consonants.

Timeline

  1. AD 57According to Chinese annals, the Han emperor grants a gold seal to an envoy from the land of Na.
  2. 471 (?)The shinkai year on the Inariyama sword, with Japanese names written phonetically; date by the prevailing interpretation.
  3. 6th centuryBuddhism reaches Japan from the Korean kingdom of Baekje, bringing Chinese sutras.
  4. late 7th centuryOfficials write on wooden mokkan tags; more than 150,000 survive.
  5. 710Heijō-kyō (Nara) becomes the capital; the Nara period begins.
  6. 712The Kojiki is completed, with 112 songs written phonetically.
  7. 720The Nihon Shoki, a chronicle in Chinese, with 128 songs in man'yōgana.
  8. after 759The Man'yōshū is compiled; its last dated poem is from 759.
  9. 783 and 788The earliest securely dated Japanese reading marks for Chinese texts.
  10. 794The capital moves to Heian-kyō (Kyoto); the Heian period begins.
  11. 806Kūkai returns from China with knowledge of the Indian Siddhaṃ script.
  12. 905The Kokin Wakashū is commissioned, with a preface written in kana.
  13. c. 935Ki no Tsurayuki writes the Tosa Diary as a woman.
  14. early 11th centuryMurasaki Shikibu writes the Tale of Genji.
  15. 1079The oldest surviving copy of the iroha poem.
  16. 1900A school reform fixes a single hiragana sign for each syllable.
